title: Broken Access Control and IDOR/BOLA
description: Learn how broken access control and IDOR/BOLA vulnerabilities expose private data. Understand vertical and horizontal access control, learn to enforce authorization in .NET APIs, and see how client-side code can accidentally leak resources.

data.text: Access control is the security backbone of every web application. It decides who can see what, who can change what, and who can delete what. When access control breaks down, users can reach data or actions that should be off-limits. The most common form of broken access control in APIs is **IDOR** — Insecure Direct Object Reference — sometimes called **BOLA** (Broken Object Level Authorization) in mobile and API contexts.

Access control failures usually come in two flavors. **Vertical access control** is about roles: an admin should be able to do things a regular user cannot, and vice versa. **Horizontal access control** is about isolation: a user should only see their own records, not records belonging to other users. When either one is missing, attackers can climb up the role ladder or reach across user boundaries.

terms.definition: When an application exposes a direct reference to an internal object (like a database ID) and fails to check whether the current user owns that object.
Restricting actions based on user roles, such as allowing only admins to delete records.
Restricting access so that users can only interact with their own data, not data belonging to other users.

data.title: Real-world impact
data.text: IDOR/BOLA was the #1 vulnerability category in the OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023). In a well-known breach, attackers enumerated sequential order IDs in an e-commerce API and downloaded thousands of customer invoices containing names, addresses, and payment details.

The safest pattern is to verify ownership inside the data-access layer. Instead of trusting the client to send the right ID, derive the allowed records from the current user's identity. Resource-based authorization in ASP.NET Core lets you attach authorization rules directly to entity instances.

data.content: This example uses resource-based authorization so that only the invoice owner or an admin can access the record.

data.text: A JavaScript frontend might hide the 'Delete' button for normal users, but that button is purely cosmetic. A determined user can open browser DevTools, replay the request, or write a one-line curl command. Authorization must be enforced on the server for every single request, regardless of what the frontend shows.

data.title: Frontend button vs real API call
data.content: The React component hides the button, but the API must still reject unauthorized access.

items.text: Verify ownership on every API endpoint that returns or modifies a single record.
items.hint: Use resource-based authorization or filter queries by the current user's ID.

items.text: Replace sequential IDs with non-guessable UUIDs for sensitive resources.
items.hint: UUIDs make enumeration harder, but do NOT replace authorization — they are an extra barrier, not a fix.

items.text: Log and alert on authorization failures.
items.hint: A spike in 403 responses often signals an active IDOR scan.

items.text: Write automated tests that swap user contexts and verify data isolation.
items.hint: If User A can access User B's record, the test should fail.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: Broken access control lets users reach data or actions outside their permissions.
IDOR/BOLA is the most common API access-control flaw and happens when servers trust client-supplied IDs.
Authorization must always be enforced server-side; frontend hiding is not a defense.
Resource-based authorization and ownership checks are the standard fix in .NET APIs.
data.takeaway: Never trust the client. Every request must be re-authorized on the server.
